IS : 7437 - 1974

Indian Standard
METHODS OF SAMPLING AND TEST FOR VEGETABLE ADHESIVES
0. FOREWORD
0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 22 November 1974, after the draft finalized by the Adhesives Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 0.2 The methods are intended to apply to adhesives manufactured from materials of vegetable origin, such as starch or materials containing a high proportion of starch, gum arabic, alginates and water-soluble ethers of cellulose. Typical examples of such adhesives are crystal gums, dextrin and water-soluble pastes and powders. This standard is not intended to apply to rubber latex or to adhesives used for mi~ccllaneous purposes, such as binders for pigments and coatings for papers. 0.3 The relative importance of the tests described depends on the purpose for which the adhesive is intended. In practice, it is customary for the user to determine by experience the most suitable type of adhesive for this purpose. The problem then reduces itself to checkmg future deliveries in respect of those properties which are relevant. Some of the physical tests, for example, the foam test, are of an empirical nature, but if these methods are carefully followed in every detail, it is possible to obtain consistent results which will give useful information both to the manufacturer and the user. 0.4 In the preparation of this standard, assistance has been obtained from BS 844 : 1965 `Methods of sampling and testing vegetable adhesives', published by the British Standards Institution. 0.5 In reporting the result of a test made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS : 2-1960*.

1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard prescribes the methods of sampling and test for adhesives It applies to adhesives in manufactured from materials of vegetable origin. the form of liquid, pastes, powders or granular solids.

4. SAMPLING 4.1 General Requirements of Sampling test samples, the 4.1.0 In drawing, following precautions preparmg, stormg and handling and directions shall be observed.

4.1.1 Precautions shall be taken to protect the samples, the material being sampled, the sampling m,trument and the contamer. Ior ,.tmples from adventitious contamination. 4.1.2 To dra*:r a representative sample, the contents of each container selected for sampling shall be mixed as thoroughly as possible bv suitable means. 4.1.3 The samples shall be placed in clean, dry, air-tight suitable containers. glass or ot!ler

4.1.4 Each sample container shall be sealed air-tight with a suitable stopper after filling, and marked with full details of sampling, the date of sampling and the year of manufacture of the material. 4.2 Scale of Sampling 4.2.1 Lot -- All the containers in a single consignment of the material of the same grade drawn from a single batch of processing shall constitute a lot. If a consignment is declared or known to consist of different batches of processing, the batches shall be marked separately and the groups of containers in ea.-h batch shall constitute separate lots. 4.2.1.1 Tests for determining the conformity of the lot to the reqmrements of the specifications shall be done on each lot separately. 4.2.2 The number of containers with co1 1 and 2 of Table 1. 5.3.1 For Solid Adhesives-Weigh into the dish to the nearest 0.001 g about 1 g of' the adhesive, ground, if necessary, to pass through 425"micron IS S&e. ~PJOTE - Yn preparing the sample for the test it shouki be remembered that the adhesive, especially in the finely divided state, may alter rapidly in moisture content according to its nature and tht: humidity of the air to whicli it is exposed. It is, therefore, important
that the operations described above should be carried out without delay and m surrotmdings which are not excessively humid or dry. There should be no delay in transferring the sample to an air-tight container pending weighing.

5.3.1.1 Renlove the cover and heat the adhesive at 105 & 2�C in the oven for 2 hours. Cover the dish, cool in a desiccator and weigh. Replace the dish in the oven, remove the cover and continue heating for 1 hour. :$.-air1 cover the dish, cool in a desiccator and weigh. Repeat the operation c,` ineating for 1 hour, cooling and weighing, until two successive weighings do not difIer by more than 0.001 g. The adhesive is then considered to be tiee from all volatile matter.

5.3.2 For Liquids and Pasies - Weigh, to the nearest 0.001 g, a quantity of the adhesive containing about 1 g of volatile-free material. A preliminary test may be made.to determine the approximate content of volatile matter. Transfer the adhesive quickly to a suitable tared dish fitted with a lid and spread it roughly over the bottom of the dish with a rod or spatula (Tvhich Replace the lid and re-weigh the dish with contents is then discarded). Heat on a boiling xvatcr-balh ,without delay. Add 10 ml of hot water. until the adhesive is homogeneous and forms a uniform thin film on the Take care to avoid any loss of contents. Contmue to bottom of the dish. heat on the boiling water-bath until the adhesive is apparently dry. 5.3.2.1 Place the dish and contents in the air-oven at 105 & 2�C and leave for 3 hours. Cover the dish, cool it in a desiccator and weigh. Replace the dish in the oven, remove the cover and continue the heating for 1 hour. Again cover the dish, cool it in a desiccator, and weigh. Repeat the operations of heatLzg for 1 hour, cooling and weighing, until two successivc weighiilgs do not differ by more than 0,001 g. The adhesive is then considered to bl: dry. 5.4 Calculation Volatile matter, percent by mass = MI -M 1

15.1.3 Procedure -- Weigh into the flask, to the nearest 0.001 g, a quantity of the adhesive containing approximately 2 g of the volatile-free material. Disperse this in approximately 30 ml of water by warming. Cool and Boil titrate with standard sulphuric acid using methyl orange as indicator. for a short time only to expel carbon dioxide, then cool and add standard sodium hydroxide solution till the mixture ,j*ust assumes a yellow tinge. Add mannitol in such proportion that the solution after titration will chntain at least 30 percent, then titrate with standard sodium hydroxide solution using phenolphthalein ar. indicator. 15.1.3.1 If the a!iaLve is very dark in colour the end point in the above titration may be obscured; it is then advisable to reduce the 2 g sample to ash before starting the determination. 15.1.4 Calculation percent by mass 348.2 x V Jv lV1) = _!U (100 Borate (as B,0,), (on dry basis)

where V = volume in ml of standard sodium hydroxide solution, N = normality of standard sodium hydroxide solution, A4 = mass in g of the sample taken for the test, and M, = percent volatile matter content of the sample (see 5).

NOTE-The presence of boric acid or metaborate is also shown by the above test. If the number of millilitres of sodium hydroxide solution consumed in the phenolphthakin titration is more than twice the number of millilitres of the sulphuric arid solution reqmred in the methyl orange titmtion, then free boric acid is present. If the number of millilitres of sodium hydroxide solution is less than twice the number of millilitres of sulphuric acid solution? some metaborate is present. If the number of millilitres of sodium hydroxide solution is equal to the number of millilitres of sulphuric acid solution, then all the borax is present as metaborate.

Procedure

15.2.3.1 Preparation of ion-exchange column - Place a small wad of cotton wool in the constriction at the foot of each of the columns. Half fil1 the columns with water and then into the first cohunn introduce the

!sr7437-1974
cation-exchange resin in the form of a slurry until a short column 3 cm high is formed. Add quantity of cation-exchange resin to the second column to a. height of 85 cm and then fill the third column in exactly the same way to a height of 35 cm with anion-exchange resin. Back wash the columns with. water and move them gently to and fro to remove air bubbles and fines. 15.2.3.2 Regeneration of the resins - In order to save time, regenerate the resins periodically in bulk. Collect 500 g quantities of the used resin and regenerate as follows:

4

Cation-exchange resin from column 2 - Introduce the resin into a glass column (2-3 cm diameter) as described above and pass 500 ml of 2 N hydrochloric acid solution through the column at a flow rate of approximately 2 ml per minute. Wash the resin with distilled water until it is free from acid. Transfer the regenerated resin into a. bottle and keep ready for further use under a layer of distilled water. Cation-exchange resin from column 1 (contaminated with `insoluble silica') Wash the resin continuously with 200 ml lots of 1 N sodium hy-droxide solution, with warming, if necessary, to remove silica. Wash the resin with water and regenerate as described in (a) above.
NOTE-The quantity of resin from column 1 is small and it may be more expedientto discard it rather than regenerate it.

b)

resin from column 3 - Regenerate c>Anion-exchange hydroxide solution in the same manner as for

with 1 N sodium the regeneration of the cationic column. Wash the resin free from alkali with distilled water, and bottle as described above, ready for future use.

15.2.3.3 Preparation of solution-Ash 20 g of the sample in a nickel Powder dish by heating over a low Bunsen flame at a low temperature. the mass with a thick glass rod and transfer it to 250-ml beaker with hot water. Cool, filter and transfer the filtrate and washing quantitatively to a 200-ml volumetric flask and dilute to volume with water. 15.2.3.4 Determination of borate -- Pipette 50 ml of the solution, prepared as described above, on to the top of the first column of the ion-exchange assembly, and allow the solution to percolate through the columns until the liquid level falls to the level of the resin in the frrst column. Elute the columns with 250 ml of water. Collect the eluate in a 500-ml conical flask, boil gently to expel carbon dioxide, cool, add three or four drops of methyl orange indicator and adjust to the first sign of a pale yellow colour by adding 0.1 N sodium hydroxide solution. Add 3-4 g of mannitol and a few drops Titrate to a pink end point with O-1 N sodium. of phenolphthalein indicator. hydroxide solution. 15.2.4 Calculation percent by mass 348.2 V JV = M (100 - Mr) *a) Borate (as BsO,), (on dv basis)

DETERMINATION

OF PROTEIN

of the Method - The adhesive is oxidized by heating with a mixture of potassium sulphate, copper sulphate and concentrated sulphuric acid, thereby converting nitrogen compounds into ammonium salts from The distilled ammonia is which ammonia is removed by distillation. absorbed in standard sulphuric acid which is then titrated with standard sodium hydroxide solution. The protein content is determined by multiplying the amount of nitrogen by 6.25.

16.3.7 Mixed Indicator Solution - Dissolve 0.1 g of methyl red and 0.05 g of methylene blue in 100 ml of rectified spirit. 16.4 Procedure-Weigh accurately about 3 g of the material in a Kjeldahl flask. Add approximately 300 mg of copper sulphate, 3 g of potassium sulphate and 25 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid. Heat the mixture gently, keeping the flask in inclined position and after frothing has ceased, boil briskly until the solutisn has remained almost colourless for 30 minutes. Cool and add 200 ml of water. Pour cautiously 50 ml of sodium hydroxide solution in the flask and then add a few pieces of pumice stone. Connect the flask to the distillation apparatus consisting of Kjeldahl connecting bulb and a condenser, the delivery tube of which extends well beneath the surface of standard sulphuric acid contained in a 500-ml flask.

21.2 Procedure - Take 50 ml of the clarified solution (see 20.2.1) in a clean Boil 400-ml flask. Add 20 ml of hydrochloric acid and 100 ml of water. gently using a water-cooled reflux condenser for two-and-a-half hours. Cool to room temperature. Neutralize the solution with sodium hydroxide solution. Transfer the solution to a 500-ml volumetric flask and make up to the mark. Determine the reducing sugar in terms of percent by mass as under 20.2. Subtract from this the percentage of reducing sugars obtained under 20.3.2 and multiply it by 0.9 to get the percentage of dextrin. 22. DETERMINATION QF GUM CONTENT

28. DETERMINATION

28.1 Application - The results of this test will be useful in assessing the foaming tendencies of adhesives, but it is not possible to simulate, in the test, all the conditions that may arise during application of the adhesives in practice. The results of the test should, therefore, be applied with caution. 28.2 Apparatus 100 ml with an air space (above the lOO-ml and 200 mm high. 28.2.1 Stoppered Glass Cylinder graduation) of 50 f 2 ml. 28.2.2 Waler-Bath -

250 mm diameter

28.3 Procedure - Disperse 5 & 0.05 g of the adhesive in slightly less than 50 ml of water, transfer the mixture to the glass cylinder and dilute to the 50-ml mark. Place the cylinder in the water-bath, maintained at a temperature of 25 f 0,2"C, so that the level of water in the bath is at the 70-ml graduation mark, and leave it for 30 minutes. At the end of this period remove the cylinder from the bath and shake it vigorously with a throw of about 300 mm and at the rate of three shakes per second for 1 minute. Then replace the cylinder in the water-bath at 25�C and allow it to remain until the height of the liquid in the cylinder corresponds to 45 ml. Record the time for this 45 ml meniscus to form, together with the volume of the foam above the liquid. NOTE - It is important that this determination from draughts.
should be carried out in a place free

27

11s: 7437 - 1974 28.4 Reporting Report both the time in minutes and the volume of loam in millilitres as either figure by itself is not a sufficient indicatron of tlr:, behaviour of the adhesive.

OF KEEPING

The rate of growth of fungi, yeasts, and bacteria is depende>: `,Lr;nong otiaer factors) upon temperature, and upon water and fungicide For this reason a solid adhesive ~111 not corice:!t;.n!ion of ;he sample. Once the solid is degener`\tr $r many years, provided that it is kept dry. dissolved m water, or a!!, existing liquid adhesive is diluted, more water is Hence available and th:~ fungi ,! re concentration (if any) is decreased. the diluted adhesi-:i: 1s more prone to growth of fungi which may impair its performance. Thertl:,Le, any test of keeping quality should be made at the concentration at which thl: adhesive will be stored or used. 29.1 Apparatus - Any spa.irlas, beakers, etc, used to transfer the adhesive and the jars used, should be clean and dry but not necessarily sterile. 29.2

of mould

OF PENTOSAN

30.0 General -

Pentosans have the general formula (C,H,O,)n and on hydrolysis by weak acid, change into pentose sugars, C,H,,O,. On boiling 28

BS : 7437 - 1974 with concentrated acid, the pentoses are decomposed with the formation of furfural. The furfural 1s precipitated by phloroglucinol as a ph.loroglucide which mav be separated by filtration, dried and weighed. Since the precipitation is not complete, a correction is made for the amount remaining in solution, using the factor 0.005 2. 30.1 Reagents 30.1.1 Phloroglucinol Retgent - Although phloroglucinol of suitaLlc purity is available, each lot shall be tested by heatin g near!y to boiling a small quantity, dissolved in a few drops of acetic anhydride, and adding a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid. A pronounced violet coloration mdicatcs the presence of diresorcin in sufficient amount to vitiate the test. `This impur iry crystallizes out if the reagent (11 g of phloroglucinol in I 500 ml of 12 percent hydrochloric acid) is prepared by first adding the phloroglucinol in small amounts with stirring to 300 ml of the hot acid and then pouring this solution into the remainder of the acid which has not been heated, allowing this to stand at least overnight. 30.1.2 H3;drochloric Acid 30.2 Procedure 12 percent (m/m).

30.2.1 Weigh out into a flask an amount of the sample sufficient to yield about 0.03 g of furfural in the process, add 100 ml of hydrochloric acid axd a few pieces of pumice stone and connect with distillation apparatus by means of a double bored rubber stopper, the second hole carrying a cylindrical separatory funnel with mark-at 30 and 60 ml. Heat at first continuou?,ly, then adjust the flame so that the distillate passing through a filter paper into a graduated cylinder will fill to the 30-m! mark in about 10 minutes. 30.2.2 Repeat the distillation, adding 30 ml of hydrochloric acid from the separatory funnel so manipulated as to wash down the sides of the flask, as many times `(usually 9 to 12) as are necessary to remove all the furfural as shown by testing with aniline acetate paper. To the joint distillate, add the phloroglucinol reagent in about double the amount required to combine with furfural from the amount of entosan judged to be present, The colour of the solution changes first to ye1Pow, then to black. Dilute to 400 ml with hydrochloric acid, allow to stand overnight, filter on a Gooch crucible or sintered crucible, wash with 150 ml of water, keeping the crucible filled with liquid until all has been added, Dry the phloroglucide and weigh. 30.3 Calculation 3.3.1 If the mass of phloroglucide a is between 0.03 and 0.30 g, calculate by the following formula: Pentosans = (a + 0.005 2) x 0.866 6 g 30.3.2 30.3.3 For mass of phloroglucide a under 0.03 g: Pentosans = (a + O-005 2) x O-899 4 g For mass of phloroglucide u over 0.30 g: Pentosans = (u + O-005 2) x O-882 4 g 29

31.0.1 Methods - Two methods have been recommended, by Redwood and Method B by Flow cup viscometers. 31.1 Method 31.11.1.1 A (Redwaod cup No. 1 Viscometer) 31.1.X Apparatus Redwood viscometer is illustrated in Fig. 3.

A

a) A cylindrical brass vessel of 2 to 3 mm wall thickness, provided with a flange at the base. The upper end of the cup is open, and has a plane rim. The bottom of the cup is concave internally to allow complete drainage of the liquid with which it may be filled. It is preferable for ease of cleaning that the internal junction of the bottom of the cup with the sides should be rounded. The flange is provided with a threaded portion 55 f 0.2 mm overall diameter by means of which the cup is supported in t.he water-bath in such a position that the top of the bore of the jet is not less than 5 mm above the upper surface of the bottom of the bath. b) The base of the cup is further provided with a tapering central hole into which the jet is fitted and cemented with its bore in the axes of the cup and its bottom surface entireIy below the adjacent metal. The oil is to be filled into the oil cup up to the level as indicated by a stout wire fixed into the side below the oil level; the sharp end of the wire is 7 f 1 mm from the inner wall of the cup. Dimensions of the cup are as follows: Internal diameter of the cup Vertical distance from rim to top of bore Height of cylindrical portion of the cup Height of filling point above upper end of bore 46.5 96.0 86.0 82.5 f + f f 0.5 mm 1 .O mm 1 ,O mm 2.0 mm

31.1.1.2 Jet - The jet is constructed of agate, and the central hole is drilled and polished to the greatest possible precision. The upper end is provided with a concave depression into which fits a ball-valve for starting or stopping the flow of adhesive. The lower end is concave to prevent the outflowing adhesive from creeping along the base of the cup. The lower end of the jet may be ground to a flat surface not exceeding 3 mm in diameter. Dimensions of the jet are as follows: Internal Internal length of the jet diameter of the jet, Min 10.0 & 0.05 mm 1.620 mm

31.2.2 Procedure - Place the flow cup on the stand in a place free from draughts, preferably with the air temperature within the range of 27 -+2"C and level by using a spirit level placed on the rim. 31.2.2.1 Strain the sample into a clean container and adjust the temperature to meet the requirements as specified in 31.0. A 150-micron IS Sieve This and the following operations (see IS : 460-1362*) or finer, is suitable. shall be carried out with minimum delay to avoid loss of solvent. 31.2.2.2 With the orifice closed by the finger, fill the cup with the bubble-free sample untri it just begins to overflow into the gallery, pouring slowly to minimize the formation of air bubbles. If bubbles are present, allow them to rise and then remove them from the surface. 31.2.2.3 Check that the temperature of the material in the cup is within 0.5"C of the test temperature. The cup may be at a temperature different from that of the sample and it is recommended that a minute or so be allowed to elapse before checking the temperature. 31.2.2.4 Place the scraper on the rim of the cup and draw it firmly Place the across until the excess o!` the sample has flowed into the gallerv. receiver under the cup.
